extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato; undergraduate/graduate philosophy students and general educated readers
extracted.subtask_description: Close commentary on Plato's educational program, the role of mathematical sciences and dialectic, stages and selection of rulers, and the political allegory (cave and regime-types) as presented in the Republic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics (arithmetic) pursued philosophically
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics 'must be pursued in the spirit of a philosopher, not of a shopkeeper. It is concerned, not with visible objects, but with abstract truth; for numbers are pure abstractions—the true arithmetician indignantly denies that his unit is capable of division.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises the purely intellectual character of arithmetic; arithmetic sharpens the wits, is a severe test of general ability, and uniquely improves even a 'stupid person.' Study should focus on pure abstraction rather than practical/commercial uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometry as elevation of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometry 'is the assistance given by it in the contemplation of the idea of good, and the compelling the mind to look at true being, and not at generation only.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometry should 'elevate the soul, and create the mind of philosophy; it should raise up what has fallen down,' not be applied merely to arts or military action. Study order: plane geometry, geometry of solids, then solids in motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomy studied by problems, not by mere star-gazing
rubrics_metrics.description: 'No one can fail to see that the contemplation of the heavens draws the soul upwards.' Yet present astronomy 'appears to me to draw the soul not upwards, but downwards'—star-gazing is mere looking at appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True astronomical study must be 'by problems' and abstract, because the heavens as seen are imperfect copies; 'Let the heavens alone, and exert the intellect'—avoid empirical illusions and focus on mathematical/dialectical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonics: seek abstract numerical harmony, not ear-based empiricism
rubrics_metrics.description: Musicians 'put their ears in the place of their minds.' Pythagorean harmonists investigate only the numbers of heard consonances and 'ascend no higher' to the unheard true numerical harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmonics should be studied abstractly (by problems) and related to the idea of the good; empirical tinkering with sounds (auscultation/tuning disputes) is criticized as missing higher import.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical sciences as a prelude to dialectic
rubrics_metrics.description: All these sciences are 'the prelude of the strain, and are profitable if they are regarded in their natural relations to one another' and to the idea of the good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematics strengthens attention, sense of order, and faculty of construction; it readies the mind for dialectic but is not itself the highest science—serves as preparatory training for intellectual sight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectic as the coping-stone and science of absolute truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialectic is 'that science which defines and explains the essence or being of each nature, which distinguishes and abstracts the good, and is ready to do battle against all opponents in the cause of good.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialectic rises above hypotheses and opinion, leads the soul from sense to contemplation of the idea of good, teaches to ask and answer questions, and is the final intellectual training necessary for rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria for rulers/guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers 'must be constant and valiant, good-looking, and of noble manners' and must 'have natural ability which education will improve; that is to say, they must be quick at learning, capable of mental toil, retentive, solid, diligent natures, who combine intellectual with moral virtues.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection emphasizes both moral and intellectual virtues, fitness for mental gymnastic trials, and excludes 'lame and one-sided' persons or those 'feeble' or 'bastard' in soul; candidates should be physically sound as well ('sound in wind and limb').

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of physical and intellectual training (avoid one-sidedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers must not be 'diligent in bodily exercise and indolent in mind, or conversely; not a maimed soul'—education must cultivate both body and mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects extremes (purely physical or purely mental specialization); the ideal guardian combines athletic discipline with sustained intellectual work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age-structured stages and timing of education
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning 'should be at first a sort of play' for the young; at twenty select promising disciples, at thirty make a further selection for withdrawal into abstraction, then 'for fifteen years let the student go down into the den, and command armies, and gain experience of life. At fifty let him return...and order his life after that pattern.' Suggested lengths: twice the time for the soul-gymnastic as for bodily gymnastics; six or perhaps five years to commence at thirty, then fifteen years of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies concrete stages and ages for training: playful early education, selective intensification at twenty and thirty, practical experience in middle life, and final return to contemplation and possible governance at fifty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid early exposure to dialectic for the young
rubrics_metrics.description: Young men are 'a sort of puppy who only plays with an argument; and is reasoned into and out of his opinions every day'—too early study of philosophy can unsettle youth and lead to skepticism and moral instability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay dialectic until maturity; early dialectical training risks producing unsettled, paradox-loving youths who bring philosophy into discredit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites for dialectic (must be disciplined in prior sciences)
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be 'no revelation of the absolute truth to one who has not been disciplined in the previous sciences'—dialectic cannot be taught without prior mathematical and scientific training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialectic requires preparatory schooling (mathematics, harmonics, geometry, etc.); it is accessible only to those who have completed the prelude disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of education for women (in the ideal State)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'You will admit that our State is not a mere aspiration, but may really come into being when there shall arise philosopher-kings...And of our governesses, for the women will share in all things with the men.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Women share equally in education and civic duties in the proposed ideal—training and roles of rulers apply to both sexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cave allegory: mapping stages of knowledge to education
rubrics_metrics.description: The cave allegory maps: shadows to the realm of fancy and poetry; images/reflections to the world of sense; mathematical abstractions to the abstractions or universals of sense; and the sun/idea of good to the highest unity from which they derive meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education should move pupils along these stages—from poetry and law, through bodily training and mathematics, to dialectic and the vision of the idea of good—mirroring ascent from illusion to true knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political meaning and practical tension of philosophical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The den or cave 'represents the narrow sphere of politics or law'—philosophers returning to the lower world may be derided and persecuted; their principles can be 'too wide for practical application' and at variance with actual conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognises a tension: the philosopher's vision may be politically impractical or disturbing; how to make the idea of good guide politics is left unexplained and is a practical problem for implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins and characteristics of timocracy (degeneration from ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Timocracy arises 'like all changes of government, from division in the rulers'; it admires warlike character, common meals, contempt for trade, and party spirit; 'arts of war begin to prevail over arts of peace' and corruption creeps into philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains social/educational causes of political degeneration: decline of education/virtue, preference of gymnastics over music, and emergence of ambition and party spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins and evils of oligarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Oligarchy arises with possession of gold and silver; 'riches outweigh virtue' and political privileges are confined to the rich. Evils include social division ('two nations...rich and poor') and perverse selection of leaders (analogy of choosing a bad pilot because he is rich).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how economic inequalities distort political selection and safety; emphasises that wealth as the criterion for rule produces instability and poor governance.
